questions.text: Change into the passive voice: The boy killed the snake.
options: The snake was killed by the boy.
The snake is killed by the boy.
The snake had been killed by the boy.
The snake was being killed by the boy.
questions.explanation: A simple past active verb (killed) becomes 'was/were + past participle' in the passive, so 'killed' becomes 'was killed'.

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: They are building a new bridge.
options: A new bridge is built by them.
A new bridge is being built by them.
A new bridge has been built by them.
A new bridge was being built by them.
questions.explanation: The present continuous active takes the passive form 'is/are being + past participle'.

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: She has finished the work.
options: The work is finished by her.
The work was finished by her.
The work has been finished by her.
The work had been finished by her.
questions.explanation: Present perfect active (has finished) becomes 'has/have been + past participle' in the passive.

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: Post the letter.
options: You are asked the letter posted.
questions.explanation: An imperative sentence is made passive with the pattern 'Let + object + be + past participle'.

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: People say that he is honest.
options: It is said that he is honest.
He is said by people honest.
It was said that he is honest.
That he is honest is saying.
questions.explanation: Sentences beginning 'People say that...' take the impersonal passive 'It is said that...'.

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: Someone stole my bicycle.
options: My bicycle is stolen by someone.
My bicycle has been stolen by someone.
questions.explanation: The past tense verb becomes 'was stolen', and an indefinite agent such as 'someone' is normally dropped in the passive.

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: Who wrote this letter?
options: Whom this letter was written by?
By whom was this letter written?
By whom this letter was written?
questions.explanation: When the interrogative 'who' is the subject, the passive question begins 'By whom' and keeps the auxiliary before the subject.

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: We must obey our elders.
options: Our elders are obeyed by us.
questions.explanation: After a modal such as 'must', the passive is formed with 'be + past participle'.

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: The gardener is watering the plants.
options: The plants are being watered by the gardener.
The plants are watered by the gardener.
The plants were being watered by the gardener.
The plants have been watered by the gardener.
questions.explanation: Present continuous active becomes 'are being watered' in the passive.

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: Has he done his duty?
options: Was his duty done by him?
Has his duty been done by him?
Is his duty done by him?
Had his duty been done by him?
questions.explanation: Present perfect interrogative takes the passive form 'Has + object + been + past participle'.

questions.text: Change into the active voice: The window was broken by the boy.
options: The boy has broken the window.
The boy had broken the window.
questions.explanation: 'Was broken' is simple past passive, so the active form keeps the simple past: 'broke'.

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: Nobody can solve this puzzle.
options: This puzzle is not solved by anybody.
This puzzle could not be solved by anybody.
This puzzle has not been solved by anybody.
This puzzle cannot be solved by anybody.
questions.explanation: A negative subject such as 'nobody' becomes 'not ... by anybody', and the modal 'can' keeps its form with 'be + past participle'.

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: The manager gave him a reward.
options: He was given a reward by the manager.
He was gave a reward by the manager.
A reward gave to him by the manager.
He has been given a reward by the manager.
questions.explanation: With a verb taking two objects, the indirect object may become the passive subject: 'He was given a reward by the manager.'

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: They had completed the project before the deadline.
options: The project was completed before the deadline.
The project had been completed by them before the deadline.
The project has been completed by them before the deadline.
The project was being completed by them before the deadline.
questions.explanation: Past perfect active (had completed) becomes 'had been + past participle' in the passive.

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: I saw him crossing the road.
options: He is seen crossing the road by me.
He was being seen crossing the road by me.
He was seen crossing the road by me.
He had been seen crossing the road by me.
questions.explanation: The simple past 'saw' becomes 'was seen', and the participle 'crossing' is retained unchanged.

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: The teacher will punish the students.
options: The students are punished by the teacher.
The students will punish by the teacher.
The students would be punished by the teacher.
The students will be punished by the teacher.
questions.explanation: The simple future active becomes 'will be + past participle'.

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: We should help the poor.
options: The poor are helped by us.
The poor must have been helped.
questions.explanation: After the modal 'should', the passive requires 'be + past participle', giving 'should be helped'.

questions.text: Change into the passive voice: Open the door.
questions.explanation: The passive of a command uses the structure 'Let + object + be + past participle'.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: He said, "I am ill."
options: He said that I am ill.
He said that he is ill.
He said that he was ill.
He said that he has been ill.
questions.explanation: After a past reporting verb the present tense shifts back to the past, and the first-person pronoun changes to the third person.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: She said to me, "I will help you."
options: She said to me that I will help you.
She said me that she will help me.
She told that she would help me.
She told me that she would help me.
questions.explanation: 'Said to me' becomes 'told me', 'will' becomes 'would', and the pronouns shift to 'she' and 'me'.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: He said, "The earth revolves round the sun."
options: He said that the earth revolves round the sun.
He said that the earth revolved round the sun.
He said that the earth had revolved round the sun.
He said that the earth would revolve round the sun.
questions.explanation: A universal truth keeps its present tense in indirect speech even after a past reporting verb.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, "Where are you going?"
options: He said to me where was I going.
He asked me where I was going.
He asked me where was I going.
He asked to me that where I was going.
questions.explanation: A reported question keeps the statement word order (subject before verb) and drops the question mark.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: He said to her, "Do you know the answer?"
options: He asked her that did she know the answer.
He said her if she knows the answer.
He asked her if she knew the answer.
He asked her does she know the answer.
questions.explanation: A yes/no question is reported with 'if' or 'whether', statement word order and a backshifted verb.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: The teacher said to the boys, "Stand up."
options: The teacher said the boys to stand up.
The teacher said that the boys stood up.
The teacher told to the boys stand up.
The teacher ordered the boys to stand up.
questions.explanation: A command is reported with a verb such as 'ordered' or 'commanded' followed by the to-infinitive.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, "Please help me."
options: He requested me to help him.
He said me please to help him.
He ordered me that I help him.
He asked me that please help him.
questions.explanation: A polite appeal containing 'please' is reported with 'requested' plus the to-infinitive.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: She said, "What a beautiful scene it is!"
options: She said that what a beautiful scene it was.
She exclaimed that it was a very beautiful scene.
She said what a beautiful scene it is.
She asked that it was a beautiful scene.
questions.explanation: Exclamatory sentences are reported with 'exclaimed', and 'what a beautiful' becomes 'a very beautiful'.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: He said, "Alas! I have lost my purse."
options: He said alas that he lost his purse.
He exclaimed with joy that he had lost his purse.
He exclaimed with sorrow that he had lost his purse.
He said that alas he has lost his purse.
questions.explanation: 'Alas' expresses grief, so it is reported as 'exclaimed with sorrow', and the present perfect backshifts to the past perfect.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, "I saw her yesterday."
options: He told me that he saw her yesterday.
He said me that he had seen her yesterday.
He told me that he has seen her the previous day.
He told me that he had seen her the previous day.
questions.explanation: The simple past backshifts to the past perfect and 'yesterday' becomes 'the previous day'.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: She said, "I shall go tomorrow."
options: She said that she would go the next day.
She said that she will go tomorrow.
She said that she would go tomorrow.
She said that she shall go the next day.
questions.explanation: 'Shall/will' becomes 'would' after a past reporting verb, and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: He said to them, "Do not make a noise."
options: He said them do not make a noise.
He forbade them to make a noise.
He told them that do not make a noise.
He asked them that they do not make a noise.
questions.explanation: A negative command is reported with 'forbade ... to' (or 'told ... not to'), followed by the infinitive.

questions.text: Change into direct speech: He said that he was busy.
questions.explanation: Reversing the backshift restores the present tense and the first-person pronoun inside the quotation marks.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, "Let us go for a walk."
options: He said me that let us go for a walk.
He told me that we go for a walk.
He asked me that we should go for a walk.
He proposed to me that we should go for a walk.
questions.explanation: 'Let us' expressing a suggestion is reported with 'proposed/suggested that we should'.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: He said to his friends, "Good morning."
options: He wished his friends good morning.
He said his friends good morning.
He told to his friends that good morning.
He greeted that it was a good morning.
questions.explanation: Greetings are reported with verbs such as 'wished' or 'greeted', without a that-clause.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: She said to him, "Thank you."
options: She told him that thank you.
She said that she thanks him.
questions.explanation: An expression of gratitude is reported simply with the verb 'thanked'.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: He said, "How foolish I am!"
options: He said how foolish he was.
He asked how foolish he was.
He exclaimed that he was very foolish.
He said that how foolish he is.
questions.explanation: 'How + adjective' in an exclamation becomes 'very + adjective' in indirect speech, reported with 'exclaimed'.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: The mother said, "May my son live long!"
options: The mother said that may her son live long.
The mother wished that her son lives long.
The mother ordered that her son should live long.
The mother prayed that her son might live long.
questions.explanation: An optative sentence is reported with 'prayed/wished that', and 'may' becomes 'might'.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: He said, "I have been waiting for an hour."
options: He said that he had been waiting for an hour.
He said that he has been waiting for an hour.
He said that he was waiting for an hour.
He said that he would be waiting for an hour.
questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous backshifts to the past perfect continuous in indirect speech.

questions.text: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, "Can you lend me your pen?"
options: He asked me that can I lend him my pen.
He asked me if I could lend him my pen.
He said me whether I can lend him my pen.
He requested me can I lend him my pen.
questions.explanation: A yes/no question takes 'if', statement word order, and 'can' backshifts to 'could'.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: If I ___ rich, I would buy a big house.
questions.explanation: The second conditional expresses an unreal present situation and uses the subjunctive 'were' with all subjects.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: If it rains tomorrow, we ___ at home.
questions.explanation: In the first conditional the if-clause takes the present simple and the main clause takes 'will + base verb'.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: If he had studied hard, he ___ the examination.
questions.explanation: The third conditional pairs 'had + past participle' in the if-clause with 'would have + past participle' in the main clause.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: Unless you work hard, you ___ succeed.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' already means 'if not', but the main clause still carries the negative outcome: you will not succeed.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: If I ___ him earlier, I would have told him the truth.
questions.explanation: A past unreal condition requires the past perfect 'had met' in the if-clause.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: Had I known the truth, I ___ you.
questions.explanation: 'Had I known' is an inverted third conditional, so the main clause needs 'would have + past participle'.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: I would have helped him if he ___ me.
questions.explanation: The main clause 'would have helped' fixes this as a third conditional, so the if-clause takes 'had asked'.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: If you heat ice, it ___.
questions.explanation: A general scientific fact takes the zero conditional: present simple in both clauses.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: Were he here, he ___ us with the arrangements.
questions.explanation: 'Were he here' is an inverted second conditional, so the main clause takes 'would + base verb'.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: If he had taken my advice, he ___ in trouble now.
questions.explanation: This is a mixed conditional: a past condition with a present result, so the main clause takes 'would not be'.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: If she ___ earlier, she would have met the minister.
questions.explanation: A third conditional if-clause requires the past perfect 'had come'.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: If I get time, I ___ you tomorrow.
questions.explanation: A real future condition uses the present simple in the if-clause and 'will + base verb' in the main clause.

questions.text: Which sentence is parallel in structure?
options: She likes swimming, dancing and to sing.
She likes to swim, dancing and singing.
She likes swimming, dancing and singing.
She likes swim, dance and singing.
questions.explanation: Items joined by 'and' must share the same grammatical form; here all three are gerunds.

questions.text: Which sentence uses the correlative pair correctly?
options: He not only is intelligent but also hardworking.
He is not only intelligent but hardworking also.
He is not only intelligent, but also he hardworking.
He is not only intelligent but also hardworking.
questions.explanation: 'Not only ... but also' must be followed by grammatically matching elements, here two adjectives.

questions.text: Complete with the parallel form: She is responsible for hiring the staff, training them and ___ their performance.
questions.explanation: The first two items are gerunds ('hiring', 'training'), so the third must also be a gerund.

questions.text: Complete with the parallel form: My duties include answering the phone, greeting visitors and ___ the mail.
questions.explanation: The list consists of gerunds, so 'sorting' preserves parallel structure.

questions.text: Complete with the parallel form: The manager wants his team to work quickly, accurately and ___.
questions.explanation: The series consists of adverbs, so the third item must also be an adverb.

questions.text: Complete with the parallel form: The post requires patience, diligence and ___.
questions.explanation: The first two items are abstract nouns, so the third must be the noun 'honesty'.

questions.text: Complete correctly: He prefers reading books to ___ television.
questions.explanation: After 'prefer ... to', both compared activities must be gerunds: 'reading ... to watching'.

questions.text: Complete with the parallel form: The committee decided to cut costs, to raise prices and ___ the staff.
questions.explanation: The series uses full infinitives, so the third item must also be 'to + base verb'.

questions.text: Complete with the parallel form: He came to the office, signed the register and ___ his seat.
questions.explanation: The three verbs share one subject and must all be in the simple past.

questions.text: Complete the sentence so that the opening phrase is not dangling: Walking down the street, ___
options: I saw the trees in full bloom.
the trees looked beautiful to me.
the trees in full bloom were seen.
questions.explanation: The introductory participle must modify the subject that follows; only 'I' can be walking down the street.

questions.text: Complete the sentence so that the opening phrase is not dangling: Having finished the work, ___
options: the television was switched on by him.
the television was on all evening.
questions.explanation: The person who finished the work must be the subject of the main clause, so 'he' must follow the participial phrase.

questions.text: Which sentence states clearly that the number of mangoes eaten was two and no more?
questions.explanation: 'Only' must stand immediately before the word it limits, so it belongs before 'two mangoes'.

questions.text: Complete the sentence so that the opening phrase is not dangling: To improve his health, ___
options: a gym membership was bought by him.
questions.explanation: An infinitive of purpose must attach to the person who has the purpose, so 'he' must be the subject.

questions.text: Complete the sentence so that the opening phrase is not dangling: Running to catch the bus, ___
options: my bag fell on the road.
questions.explanation: Only a person can run to catch a bus, so the main clause must begin with 'I'.

questions.text: Which sentence makes clear that the man, not the police, was wearing a mask?
options: The man was arrested by the police wearing a mask.
The man wearing a mask was arrested by the police.
Wearing a mask, the police arrested the man.
The man was wearing a mask arrested by the police.
questions.explanation: A modifying phrase should sit next to the noun it describes, so 'wearing a mask' must follow 'the man'.

questions.text: Which version corrects the dangling modifier in 'At the age of five, my mother enrolled me in school'?
options: At five years of age, my mother enrolled me in school.
My mother, at the age of five, enrolled me in school.
When I was five, my mother enrolled me in school.
At the age of five, school was where my mother enrolled me.
questions.explanation: The original wrongly makes the mother five years old; replacing the phrase with a clause naming 'I' removes the error.

questions.text: Complete the sentence so that the opening phrase is not dangling: After reading the original study, ___
options: there was little to convince anyone.
questions.explanation: The reader must be the subject of the main clause, otherwise the article appears to have read the study.

questions.text: Which sentence makes clear that the sandwiches, not the children, were on paper plates?
options: She served sandwiches to the children on paper plates.
She served the children sandwiches on paper plates.
On paper plates she served the children sandwiches.
She served the children on paper plates sandwiches.
questions.explanation: Placing 'sandwiches' immediately before 'on paper plates' attaches the phrase to the food rather than to the children.

questions.text: Which is the correct possessive form for books belonging to children?
questions.explanation: 'Children' is already an irregular plural, so the possessive adds apostrophe + s.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: The dog wagged ___ tail.
questions.explanation: 'Its' is the possessive determiner; 'it's' is the contraction of 'it is'.

questions.text: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
options: I have a meeting at noon; therefore, I cannot join you.
I have a meeting at noon, therefore I cannot join you.
I have a meeting at noon therefore, I cannot join you.
I have a meeting at noon: therefore I cannot join you.
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses linked by the conjunctive adverb 'therefore' require a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

questions.text: The speaker has only one brother. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: My brother who lives in Lahore is a doctor.
My brother, who lives in Lahore, is a doctor.
My brother, who lives in Lahore is a doctor.
My brother who lives in Lahore, is a doctor.
questions.explanation: A non-defining relative clause adds extra information and must be enclosed by a pair of commas.

questions.text: Which sentence uses quotation marks and punctuation correctly?
options: He said, I am going home.
questions.explanation: A comma introduces the quotation, the first word is capitalised, and the full stop falls inside the closing quotation marks.

questions.text: Which sentence punctuates the introduction of the list correctly?
options: She bought three things, bread, milk and eggs.
She bought three things; bread, milk and eggs.
She bought three things - bread; milk; and eggs.
She bought three things: bread, milk and eggs.
questions.explanation: A colon introduces a list that follows a complete independent clause.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: ___ book is lying on the table?
questions.explanation: 'Whose' is the possessive interrogative; 'who's' means 'who is'.

questions.text: Which sentence is punctuated to show that the speaker is addressing Grandma?
questions.explanation: A comma must separate a noun of address from the rest of the sentence.

questions.text: Which sentence is correctly hyphenated?
options: He is a well known writer.
questions.explanation: A compound adjective placed before the noun it modifies takes a hyphen.

questions.text: Which sentence avoids a comma splice?
options: It was getting late, we went home.
It was getting late we went home.
It was getting late, we, went home.
It was getting late, so we went home.
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone; a coordinating conjunction such as 'so' is needed.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: Neither of the boys ___ present in the class.
questions.explanation: 'Neither' used as a pronoun is singular and takes a singular verb.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: The quality of the mangoes ___ not good.
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular noun 'quality'; the prepositional phrase 'of the mangoes' does not change the number.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: Each of the students ___ been given a book.
questions.explanation: 'Each' is always singular and takes a singular verb regardless of the plural noun that follows.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: Ten miles ___ a long distance to walk.
questions.explanation: A plural expression of distance, weight or money treated as a single unit takes a singular verb.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: The news ___ very encouraging.
questions.explanation: 'News' is an uncountable noun that is singular in form and meaning despite the final -s.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: Mathematics ___ my favourite subject.
questions.explanation: Names of subjects ending in -ics take a singular verb.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: One of my friends ___ a doctor in Karachi.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'one', which is singular; 'of my friends' merely limits it.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: Neither he nor his brothers ___ coming to the party.
questions.explanation: With 'neither ... nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, which here is the plural 'brothers'.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: A number of students ___ absent today.
questions.explanation: 'A number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb, unlike 'the number of', which is singular.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: Bread and butter ___ my usual breakfast.
questions.explanation: Two nouns naming one combined item take a singular verb.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: Politics ___ not an easy profession.
questions.explanation: 'Politics' as a field of activity is singular and takes a singular verb.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: The scissors on the table ___ very sharp.
questions.explanation: Nouns naming instruments made of two parts, such as scissors, are always plural in construction.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: He has been living in this house ___ 2010.
questions.explanation: 'Since' is used with a point in time, while 'for' is used with a length of time.

questions.text: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
questions.explanation: A finished time expression such as 'yesterday' requires the simple past, not the present perfect.

questions.text: Choose the correct form: He said that he ___ come the next day.
questions.explanation: After a past reporting verb, 'will' changes to 'would' under the sequence of tenses.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: Hardly had I reached the station ___ the train left.
questions.explanation: 'Hardly' is followed by 'when'; only 'no sooner' takes 'than'.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: No sooner did he see the police ___ he ran away.
questions.explanation: 'No sooner' is a comparative form and is always followed by 'than'.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: It is three years ___ he left the country.
questions.explanation: The pattern 'It is + period of time + since + past tense' expresses how long ago something happened.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: He is senior ___ me by two years.
questions.explanation: Latin comparatives such as senior, junior, superior and inferior take 'to', never 'than'.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: He prefers tea ___ coffee.
questions.explanation: The verb 'prefer' is followed by 'to' when two things are compared.

questions.text: Choose the correct completion: We shall discuss ___ at tomorrow's meeting.
questions.explanation: 'Discuss' is a transitive verb and takes a direct object without any preposition.

questions.text: Which sentence is free from redundancy?
options: He returned back home late at night.
He repeated the same thing again.
He returned home late at night.
He reverted back to his old habits.
questions.explanation: 'Return' already contains the idea of 'back', so adding 'back' is redundant.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: She could not cope ___ the pressure of work.
questions.explanation: The verb 'cope' is always followed by the preposition 'with'.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: His opinion is quite different ___ mine.
questions.explanation: 'Different' is standardly followed by 'from' in formal written English.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: She is married ___ a civil servant.
questions.explanation: A person is 'married to' another person; 'married with' is incorrect.

questions.text: Choose the correct completion: The committee ___ ten members.
questions.explanation: 'Comprise' means 'consist of' and is used without a preposition.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: This matter must remain a secret between you and ___.
questions.explanation: A pronoun following a preposition must be in the objective case, so 'me' is required.

questions.text: Which sentence uses the comparative degree correctly?
options: He is more intelligent than his brother.
He is more cleverer than his brother.
He is most intelligent than his brother.
He is intelligenter than his brother.
questions.explanation: A comparative is formed either with '-er' or with 'more', never with both, and three-syllable adjectives take 'more'.

questions.text: Choose the correct word: He is the ___ of the two brothers.
questions.explanation: When only two persons are compared, the comparative degree 'elder' is used, not the superlative.

questions.text: Choose the correct verb: Every boy and girl of the school ___ given a prize.
questions.explanation: Nouns joined by 'and' but preceded by 'every' or 'each' are treated as singular.

questions.text: Choose the correct completion: He is not only a poet ___ a novelist of repute.
questions.explanation: 'Not only' pairs exclusively with 'but also' as a correlative conjunction.

questions.text: Choose the correct completion: Neither the principal ___ the teachers were present at the function.
questions.explanation: 'Neither' is always followed by 'nor' in a correlative pair.

questions.text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: The number of students / in the class / are increasing / every year.
questions.explanation: 'The number of' takes a singular verb, so it should read 'is increasing'.

questions.text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: One of my friend / is coming / to my house / tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'One of' must be followed by a plural noun, so the phrase should be 'one of my friends'.

questions.text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: He is / more cleverer / than / his brother.
questions.explanation: A double comparative is wrong; the correct form is simply 'cleverer'.

questions.text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: The boy who / was standing / near the gate / have gone away.
questions.explanation: The singular subject 'the boy' requires 'has gone away'.

questions.text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: She is junior / than me / by two years / in service.
questions.explanation: 'Junior' takes the preposition 'to', so the phrase should be 'junior to me'.

questions.text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: The furnitures / in the new office / were bought / last month.
questions.explanation: 'Furniture' is an uncountable noun and has no plural form.

questions.text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: She has a lot of / informations / about the new policy / of the government.
questions.explanation: 'Information' is uncountable and is never used in the plural.

questions.text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: I am looking forward / to meet you / at the conference / next week.
questions.explanation: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition and must be followed by a gerund: 'to meeting you'.

questions.text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: We discussed / the whole matter / but could not / arrive to a conclusion.
questions.explanation: The idiom is 'arrive at a conclusion', not 'arrive to'.

questions.text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: The manager, / along with his assistants, / were present / at the meeting.
questions.explanation: A phrase introduced by 'along with' does not change the number of the subject, so the verb must be 'was present'.
